blocks.text: 1. LSTM Architecture
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742497-237072736.png

The Exploding Gradient Problem, the final topic of the previous RNN module, closed out coverage of that module's two core training challenges. LSTM Architecture opens the LSTM & GRU module, an architecture specifically designed to address both gradient problems.

Long Short-Term Memory works specifically to address both gradient problems already covered in the previous module, a genuinely important architectural response explored throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping The Problems Being Solved

This connects back to a preview of the solution, already covered in The Vanishing Gradient Problem. LSTM was specifically designed to directly address the vanishing gradient problem already covered there.

This happens while Gradient Clipping, already covered, separately handled the exploding gradient side, together forming a genuinely complete response to both problems covered throughout the entire previous module.
3. The Cell State Idea
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742498-157460043.png

LSTM's genuinely core innovation connects back to the hidden state, already covered in its own topic. A genuinely separate cell state runs alongside the hidden state, acting as a genuinely more protected memory channel.
This genuinely distinguishes LSTM from Vanilla RNN, already covered, which relied on the hidden state alone as its own single memory mechanism.

blocks.text: 4. The Gates Concept, Introduced
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742498-38490180.png
This connects back to the hidden state as memory, already covered in Hidden State. LSTM genuinely introduces gates: small networks that decide what information to keep, add, or output.

These are covered individually in complete depth across the next three topics of this module, giving LSTM a genuinely deliberate, learnable way to manage its own memory rather than relying on a single, fixed update rule.
5. A Quick Preview Of All Three Gates

A genuinely quick preview covers all three gates at once. The forget gate decides what to genuinely discard from the cell state, already covered as the genuinely first gate covered in its own dedicated topic.

The input gate decides what genuinely new information to add; the output gate decides what to genuinely reveal as the hidden state, both covered in their own complete, dedicated topics later in this module.
6. The Sigmoid Gating Mechanism
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742498-752625263.png

This connects back to Sigmoid, already covered in the Activation Functions module. Every gate genuinely uses Sigmoid to produce a value between 0 and 1, directly reusing that earlier activation function.

This acts as a genuinely smooth, learnable on-off switch for information flow, letting each gate genuinely control how much information passes through, rather than a genuinely abrupt, all-or-nothing decision.

blocks.text: 7. Why The Cell State Genuinely Helps With Gradients

blocks.alt: Why The Cell State Genuinely Helps With Gradients
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742499-83159907.png

This connects back to the long chain of multiplication, already covered in The Vanishing Gradient Problem. The cell state genuinely allows information to flow with mostly genuinely additive, rather than purely multiplicative, updates.
This directly reduces the genuinely severe shrinkage already covered throughout that earlier topic, since additive updates do not compound the same way repeated multiplication by values below 1 does.
8. More Parameters Than Vanilla RNN
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742499-989139576.png
This connects back to parameter count, already covered generally throughout this course. An LSTM genuinely has considerably more parameters than a Vanilla RNN of the same hidden size.
This is a genuinely real, honest cost directly resulting from the multiple gates already covered in this topic, each requiring its own genuinely separate set of learnable weights.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When LSTM Is Genuinely The Right Choice

blocks.alt: Recognizing When LSTM Is Genuinely The Right Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742499-785335556.png

This connects back to long-range dependencies, already covered as Vanilla RNN's own genuine weakness. LSTM's own cell state and gates, already covered in this topic, directly address that exact weakness.
Tasks genuinely needing to remember far earlier context reliably are another genuine case where LSTM, already covered, remains a genuinely strong, well-established choice.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates the genuinely conceptual structure of an LSTM cell, showing the cell state and hidden state evolving together across a few time steps, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
hidden_size = 4

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

def lstm_step(x_t, h_prev, c_prev, rng):
    # a genuinely simplified sketch of the three gates already previewed in this topic
    forget_gate = sigmoid(rng.normal(size=hidden_size) * 0.5)   # already covered as a preview in this topic
    input_gate = sigmoid(rng.normal(size=hidden_size) * 0.5)
    output_gate = sigmoid(rng.normal(size=hidden_size) * 0.5)
    candidate_values = np.tanh(rng.normal(size=hidden_size) * 0.5)

    c_t = forget_gate * c_prev + input_gate * candidate_values  # already covered as the cell state idea in this topic
    h_t = output_gate * np.tanh(c_t)
    return h_t, c_t

hidden_state = np.zeros(hidden_size)
cell_state = np.zeros(hidden_size)
sequence = [rng.normal(size=hidden_size) for _ in range(4)]

for t, x_t in enumerate(sequence):
    hidden_state, cell_state = lstm_step(x_t, hidden_state, cell_state, rng)
    print(f"Time step {t}: cell state = {np.round(cell_state, 3)}, hidden state = {np.round(hidden_state, 3)}")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: LSTM, Long Short-Term Memory, is specifically designed to address both gradient problems from the previous module.
A separate cell state runs alongside the hidden state, acting as a more protected memory channel.
LSTM introduces gates: small networks deciding what information to keep, add, or output.
The forget, input, and output gates each play their own distinct role, covered individually next.
Every gate uses Sigmoid to produce a smooth, learnable on-off switch for information flow.
The cell state allows mostly additive updates, directly reducing vanishing gradient shrinkage.
An LSTM has considerably more parameters than a Vanilla RNN of the same hidden size.
It remains a strong, well-established choice for tasks needing to remember far earlier context.
Next up: The Forget Gate, a complete, dedicated look at LSTM's first gate.
